activities.anchor: If it has more unknowns than equations
activities.caption: run the budget check — can statics finish alone?
activities.name: ceDetermBranch

config.root: You are handed a structure and its supports. How do you know whether statics alone can finish the job?

start.text: Count first: how many unknown support forces, against how many equilibrium statements?

choices.label: Three unknowns, three statements in 2-D
choices.feedback: The budget matches — solve ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0, ΣM = 0 and every reaction falls out.

choices.label: More unknowns than statements
choices.feedback: Equilibrium alone cannot close it — material stiffness must be invited in.

determinate.text: Statically determinate: statics finds every reaction. Cut the members and equilibrium still holds, exposing axial force, shear and bending moment.

indeterminate.text: Indeterminate — a continuous beam over several supports, a rigid frame. What closes the surplus?

choices.label: Deformations: members must deflect together
choices.feedback: Compatibility plus stiffness — and stiffer members attract more load, which is why differential settlement matters more than novices expect.

compat.text: Material stiffness and compatibility of deformation close the surplus — the gateway from second-year mechanics to real design.

config.why: Three per body is the hard budget in two dimensions: match it and statics finishes; exceed it and stiffness must join.

activities.anchor: A structure needs ΣM = 0 as well as ΣF = 0
activities.caption: true or false — the balance trap
activities.name: ceMomentJudge

statements.s: If the vertical forces balance, everything is fine.
statements.why: Forces can cancel while turning effects do not — the second condition is about the twist, not the push.

statements.s: Two equal, opposite forces on either side of a steering wheel produce zero net force and still spin it furiously.
statements.why: A pure couple: zero net force, maximum turning effect.

statements.s: A crane's counterweight is there to add upward force.
statements.why: Its job is cancelling turning effects — placement, not push.

statements.s: The moment of a force is the force times the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the force's line.
statements.why: M = r·F — the see-saw rule and the door hinge are the same arithmetic.

activities.anchor: each bar carries force only along its own axis
activities.caption: file each member by what it does
activities.name: ceTrussSort

config.prompt: File each member by what it does:

items.label: the rafters under the apex load
the horizontal tie at the apex
the cable stays of a suspension span
the vertical hangers of a suspension bridge
the ring of a masonry arch

config.why: A pin joint can pull or push but never bend — that is what turns a tangle of steel into pure arithmetic.

activities.anchor: exploits this one pin at a time
activities.caption: put the apex working in order
activities.name: ceJointsOrder

config.prompt: One apex, two rafters at 30°, a horizontal tie, a 10 kN load — put the working in order:
items: Isolate the apex joint — two unknown bar forces, two useful statements
Vertical equilibrium: two rafters × sin 30° must carry 10 kN — each rafter pushes with 10 kN
The rafters are in compression — they will need buckling checks
Horizontal equilibrium: the tie pulls with 10 × cos 30° ≈ 8.7 kN
The tie is in tension — strength only, no buckling check
config.why: Each pin is a small body in equilibrium — three members, one apex, three sentences of algebra.

activities.anchor: Now stand it the other way
activities.caption: call the stiffness of the joist on edge
activities.name: ceJoistEst

config.prompt: A 100 mm × 200 mm timber joist stands on edge (I = b·h³/12 about the horizontal axis). Roughly what is its second moment of area?
config.why: About 66.7 × 10⁶ mm⁴ — laid flat it collapses to 16.7 × 10⁶, four times less stiffness from the same plank, same weight.
config.context: Depth enters cubed: growing 200 mm to 400 mm multiplies I by 2³ = 8 — the whole secret of the I-beam.

activities.anchor: Plot that moment along the span and you have the single most informative drawing
activities.caption: pair each diagram feature with its design use
activities.name: ceDiagramMatch

config.prompt: Read the diagram like a designer — pair each feature with its use:

pairs.right: the maximum demand the worst section must carry
peak drops from P·L/4 to w·L²/8 — half the value

pairs.left: a heavier, misplaced load discovered after the fact
pairs.right: what many failure investigations reduce to

config.why: Every load case draws its own diagram, and the design must survive the envelope of all of them.

activities.caption: slide to the frequency floors must clear
activities.name: ceFloorPlace

config.prompt: Pedestrians walk at 1.6–2.4 steps per second, with harmonics at two and three times that. Slide the marker to the frequency guidance pushes rhythmic-occupancy floors above.
config.why: About 7.5 Hz — not so the floor is stronger, but so the crowd cannot find their rhythm. The worked floor sits at ≈6.4 Hz: above a brisk walk's second harmonic, but not comfortably.

activities.caption: drag the divider across the two regimes
activities.name: ceRegimesCompare

config.prompt: The same three equations, with and without inertia — drag the divider:

before.label: statics
before.text: Bodies never accelerate: zero net force and zero net moment, three statements per body — a parked truck loads the deck no harder than it weighs.

after.label: dynamics
after.text: Add mass × acceleration: rolling trucks arrest suspension and hit harder (amplification often ~1.3), and rhythmic loads pump energy at natural frequencies.

config.why: Same three equations, new inertia terms — and suddenly crowds can walk a deck into swaying.
